what_its_for: Chloroquine is used to prevent and treat malaria, a serious infection spread by mosquito bites. It is also used to treat a condition called extraintestinal amebiasis, which is an infection caused by a parasite that can affect the liver. In some cases, doctors may prescribe it for certain autoimmune conditions like lupus or rheumatoid arthritis.
how_to_take: Take chloroquine by mouth, exactly as your doctor prescribed. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. It is best to take it with food or milk to help prevent an upset stomach. If you are taking it to prevent malaria, start taking it before you travel, continue during your trip, and keep taking it for the full time after you return home, as your doctor directed. Do not stop taking it early, even if you feel well.
dosing: Your dose will depend on what condition is being treated, your weight, and your kidney function. For malaria prevention in adults, a common dose is 500 mg (300 mg base) once a week, taken on the same day each week. For treating malaria, the dose is higher and taken over 2 to 3 days. For children, the dose is based on body weight. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store chloroquine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets. Chloroquine can be very dangerous if accidentally swallowed by a child, even in small amounts. Dispose of unused or expired medication safely — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids or kaolin (found in some anti-diarrhea products) within 4 hours of taking chloroquine, as they can reduce how well this medicine works. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it may increase the risk of side effects on your liver. Be careful with activities that require sharp vision or good balance if you experience dizziness or vision changes. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as chloroquine may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, as chloroquine can interact with many drugs including heart medications and other antimalarials.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: sudden vision changes or blurred vision, seeing halos around lights, muscle weakness or difficulty walking, irregular or fast heartbeat, chest pain, seizures, severe dizziness or fainting, unusual mood changes, depression, or thoughts of self-harm, hearing loss or ringing in the ears, yellowing of the skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also contact your doctor if your malaria symptoms do not improve after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: If you are taking chloroquine to treat malaria, you should start feeling better within 1 to 2 days of starting treatment. If you are using it to prevent malaria, it works as long as you take it correctly — before, during, and after travel. For autoimmune conditions like lupus, it may take several weeks to months before you notice improvement. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you do not notice effects right away.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Chloroquine can be used to prevent and treat malaria during pregnancy when the benefit outweighs the risk — talk to your doctor. Children: Doses are based on body weight; children are especially sensitive to overdose, so keep this medicine safely stored away from them. Older adults: Use with caution, as older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially heart and vision problems. Kidney or liver disease: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver problems. People with G6PD deficiency (a blood disorder): Chloroquine may rarely cause breakdown of red blood cells in these patients — tell your doctor if you have this condition. People with psoriasis or porphyria: Chloroquine may worsen these conditions and is generally not recommended.
